newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian stocks leap ahead on record Dow rise.
newsitem.headline: Asian stocks leap ahead on record Dow rise.

text.p: Most Asian stock markets, led by Japan, bounded ahead on Tuesday on the back of Wall Street's all-time closing high.

Shares in Tokyo pushed through the key 20,000-point barrier and Sydney's All Ordinaries reached a record but Thailand closed at a 5-1/2 year low. South Korea also failed to capture the enthusiasm and headed lower.
The Dow gained 143 points, or 2.03 percent, to 7,214 on Monday on expectations of a cut in the capital gains tax and a belief that any further interest rate increases would be modest.

The 225-share Nikkei average jumped 666.17 points or 3.41 percent -- its second-largest one-day gain this year -- to end at 20,180.92, the highest closing level since 20,413.46 set on December 17. The market was closed on Monday.
"Worries over downside risks have diminished recently..., and the U.S. stocks' surge lifted the Nikkei..." said Hisao Suzuki, deputy general manager at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd.

"Rounds of buying in issues which were far behind the popular blue chips, such as some financials and domestic demand-sensitive shares, in addition to bellwether issues, powered the market higher," said Noboru Yorita, general manager at Tachibana Securities Co Ltd.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index ended 180.00 points, or 1.34 percent, higher to 13,579.34 after reaching a high of 13,679.92.
"Sentiment in the Dow has turned around," said Peter Lai, associate director at OCBC Securities.
"And people believe that there will be no interest rate increase this month," he said.
However, traders were divided over how much further the market could advance or whether it will fall victim to profit-taking.
"It is likely that the market will stay at current levels and I think at this level people should take profit," said Sunny Chan, senior research manager at Seapower Securities.
Wall Street's advance also helped boost Philippine stocks after more than a week of sharp declines. Fresh domestic economic data buoyed sentiment.
Philippine stocks gained 40.11 points, or 1.47 percent, to close at 2,776.53.

Traders said the overall bearish sentiment that had gripped the Philippine market for more than a week had ebbed. Monday's better-than-expected inflation figures and solid trade data on Tuesday helped underpin the advance.
Singapore stocks followed the Dow and added 27.08 points, or 1.33 percent. The Straits Times Index ended at 2,055.68.
"The market has been oversold and investors are just looking for something to buy," said one dealer.

Indonesian shares closed 6.81 points, or 1.04 percent, higher at 659.60 on the back of the Dow, while Taiwan shares defied a bout of profit-taking and ended up 24.84 points, or 0.30 percent, at 8,294.27.
Australian stocks finished at a record high of 2,512.8, led by gains in New York and Tokyo, The All Ordinaries Index ended up 20.1 points, or 0.81 percent.
But some markets bucked the trend.

Thai shares closed 16.82 points, or 2.55 percent, lower after opening higher on speculation that March export figures could show some improvement. The SET Index finished at 643.28, its lowest close since November 1, 1991.
Brokers blamed lingering market concerns over the sluggish Thai economy and weak corporate earnings.
South Korean stocks ignored Wall Street, closing lower as blue chips fell, but paper and pharmaceutical makers rose on bargain hunting, brokers said.
The composite index ended 3.30 points, or 0.47 percent, lower at 701.57.
